title: Ghosts, a stolen skull and a haunted castle lurk in this New Zealand city
excerpt: Spooky Dunedin leans in to its Celtic past.
content:
Spooky Dunedin leans in to its Celtic past.

Larnach Castle. Picture by Tourism NZ

By Julie Miller

November 22, 2026

As I follow a shadowy figure wearing a top hat and black coat through the gates of Dunedin's Northern Cemetery, my jacket catches on a sprig of hawthorn, planted as a hedge to form the boundary fence.

"Careful, don't break that," the ghoulish visage warns me. "It's considered bad luck to snap a twig or branch of hawthorn, that's a big thing with the fairies."

Fairies? I thought I was here to look for spirits of a more sinister nature, following the distinctively dressed Andrew Smith from Hair Raiser Tours through one of his favourite Dunedin haunts. But it seems in cemeteries like this, created in the superstitious Victorian era, ghosts and fairies are closely intertwined, with the Celtic mythology of Dunedin's original Scottish and Irish settlers expressed through symbolism.

Hawthorn hedges, Smith continues, were planted as a protective barrier from negative energy, with the prickly bushes symbolising the gateway to the fairy realm. Throughout the cemetery we'll also walk past other plants loaded with hidden meaning - yew trees, representing rebirth and resurrection; a monkey puzzle tree, planted to prevent the devil from stealing souls; and heritage roses, honouring purity and heavenly perfection.

"Every plant had a symbolic meaning that related back to the ancient language of the trees, known as 'Ogham'," Smith says. "Every tree in here has some sort of spiritual meaning."

Clinging to a volcanic hillside like a brooding raincloud, New Zealand's South Island city of Dunedin - known to its original Maori inhabitants as Otepoti - was chosen as a planned settlement of the Lay Association of the Free Church of Scotland in 1848. Named after the Scottish Gaelic word for Edinburgh, Dun Èiddean, its residents continue to embrace these Celtic roots, with gestures such as its own tartan, a statue of Scottish bard Robbie Burns in the central Octagon and an annual highland games and arts festivals.

Tour guide Andrew Smith.

Even its cityscape bears a resemblance to its northern namesake, with distinctive neo-gothic structures such as the "gingerbread house" Dunedin Railway Station and the Oamaru limestone First Church of Otago considered the best-preserved examples of Victorian architecture in the southern hemisphere.

But the quirky Gaelic influence runs deeper than bricks and mortar. Its youthful, creative population appears to have a penchant for the macabre, typified by the success of Smith's Hair Raiser Tours, which has offered several spooky walks throughout the city since 1999.

Dunedin is also home to one of the weirdest little museums imaginable, the mindboggling Museum of Natural Mystery. Located in a Victorian terrace house, this lifetime collection of artist and former "Dunedin sound" musician Bruce Mahalksi features "biological curiosities, ethnological art and unusual cultural artifacts", including Mahalski's rather terrifying sculptural creations made from animal skulls and bones.

Inside Larnach Castle. Picture by Tourism NZ

The darkest of Dunedin's attractions, however, is also one of its most picturesque - a turreted edifice located on the rolling green hills of the Otago Peninsula known as Larnach Castle. Dating to 1871, this impeccably restored mansion offers an insight into Victorian finery, with guided tours, dinner experiences, high teas and on-site accommodation showcasing gorgeous period furniture and sprawling landscaped gardens.

But as I indulge in a decadent spread of scones, cucumber sandwiches and sweets in the castle's grand ballroom after a guided tour, I can't help but be unsettled by the castle's tragic history, a story that has contributed to its reputation as one of New Zealand's most haunted places.

Designed by prominent architect Robert Lawson, this gothic revival masterpiece was meant to be the crown jewel for prominent businessman and politician William Larnach, a symbol of his great wealth and community status. But tragedy soon marred this happy family home. In 1880, Larnach's wife Eliza Jane died of an apoplectic fit, followed several years later by her half-sister Mary, whom Larnach had married in 1882.

Graveyard rose.

Then, after his beloved daughter Kate fell victim to typhoid in 1891, Larnach discovered that his third wife, Constance, was having an affair with his son Douglas. Overwrought with grief, Larnach, with a single bullet to the temple, ended his misery in New Zealand's Parliament buildings in 1898. Twelve years later, his oldest son Donald followed suit, and joined his tragic family interred in a lavish tomb in the Northern Cemetery.

It's impossible to miss this ostentatious crypt - the largest in the southern hemisphere - during Smith's ghost tour, gleaming under spotlights on a prominent hillside in the eight-hectare graveyard. And if the spired structure looks familiar, that's because the tomb is, in fact, a scale replica of Robert Lawson's First Church, located within distant eyesight in Dunedin's CBD.

"William Larnach loved the church so much he wanted to replicate it," Smith says. "But there's an irony here with the Larnach family - even in death they are not left alone." For many years, Smith continues, people have visited the tomb to gawk, and in some cases vandalise it. In 1972, a group of partying university students broke into the tomb, desecrating the graves and scattering bones through the cemetery.

"In the shenanigans, William Larnach's skull was stolen," Smith says. "It was recovered several years later, being used as an ashtray in a student household. That's Dunedin for you!"

TRIP NOTES

Explore verdict: Hair Raiser Tours add colour and context to this fascinating city, its gothic architecture and Celtic roots.

Getting there: Air New Zealand has direct flights from Sydney to Christchurch. The Mainlander train travels between Christchurch and Invercargill, with overnight stops in Dunedin.

Where to stay: The Mainlander's Rail and Stay package includes three nights' accommodation in Distinction Dunedin Hotel (or similar) and is priced from $NZ1026 ($838) per person.

Good to know: There is no public transport to Larnach Castle, car hire is recommended. While on the Otago Peninsula, don't miss the Royal Albatross Centre and its wildlife tours. albatross.org.nz

See + do: Hair Raiser Tours' Northern Cemetery Tour is $NZ60. A guided tour of Larnach Castle costs $NZ78. hairraisertours.com; larnachcastle.co.nz

Explore more: dunedinnz.com; themainlander.co.nz

The writer travelled as a guest of Enterprise Dunedin and The Mainlander
